Cineplex Appoints Bill Walker CEO, Mulls Sale of Business
Cineplex has appointed Bill Walker to take over the lead role from retiring long-time chief executive Ellis Jacob, and said it is considering a sale as part of a newly launched strategic review.

Walker brings to the Canadian movie theater chain a wealth of experience in retail and entertainment. He was previously CEO of Landmark Cinemas, another Canadian theater chain which sold to Belgium-based Kinepolis Group in 2017.

At the same time, the company has announced that it has launched a strategic review to evaluate new opportunities to maximize value for its shareholders. Cineplex said it will consider a range of alternatives, which could include a potential sale, among others. Jacob is expected to work with the board on the review.
Saputo Restructures Operating Units, Forms Dedicated Ingredients Division
Saputo has restructured its leadership and operating units, including with the creation of a new ingredients division, to accelerate expansion of its capabilities in higher-margin dairy products.
The organizational realignment comes as the Montreal-based dairy producer pivots toward specialized protein ingredients and focuses on expansion across global commercial markets.

Under the new structure, Saputo said Wednesday that it has appointed Steve Douglas as chief operating officer of the ingredients business. He is currently COO of the company's U.K. dairy division, and will remain in that role until sale of the unit is complete, the company said.
AGF Management Third-Quarter Profit, Revenue Rise
AGF Management reported a rise in third-quarter profit and revenue, driven by higher management fees and assets under management.
The asset management firm posted net income of C$31.2 million, or C$0.48 a share, for the third quarter ended Aug. 31, up from C$28.4 million, or C$0.42 a share, in the comparable quarter a year ago.
Total adjusted net revenues rose to C$112.5 million from C$107.5 million. The company benefited from higher net management, advisory and administration fees of C$101 million, up from C$88.8 million.
Quantum eMotion Gains on SecureKey Patent Progress, U.S.-Canada Compliance Review

Shares of Quantum eMotion rose after it said it has received a key U.S. patent approval for its core data-security technology while advancing the software through compliance testing in Canada and the U.S.
Shares rose nearly 15% to C$2.86.

The company said Wednesday that it has received a notice of allowance from the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office for its SecureKey technology, a cryptographic technology designed to secure encryption keys while in active use.
Global Atomic Shares Slide on Discounted C$50 Million Public Offering
Shares of Global Atomic fell sharply after the company priced a C$50 million public offering, diluting existing shareholders.
Shares dropped 16% to C$0.45.

The Canadian uranium company is raising money to continue developing its Dasa project in Niger, which it says will give it time to assess how to fund the remaining gap before drawing down on its U.S. International Development Finance contribution.
Maple Leaf Foods to Shut Down Two U.S. Plants in Consolidation Effort
Maple Leaf Foods plans to consolidate its U.S. plant protein production into a single site in Indianapolis.
The consolidation will include winding down production at plants in Seattle and Turners Falls, Mass., the Canadian consumer packaged goods company said.

Maple Leaf plans to execute the transition over about 12 to 18 months, with targeted completion in the fourth quarter of 2027. Production will continue in Seattle and Turners Falls during the transition period.
Canada's Population Growth Continues to Slow, Hits Estimated 41.8 Million

Canada's population grew only marginally in the latest quarter, with numbers swelling at the lowest pace since World War II and by less than when border restrictions were in place to combat the spread of Covid-19.

The country's population hit an estimated just under 41.8 million on July 1, a rise of 189,425 people, or 0.5%, on a year earlier, Statistics Canada said. The population grew by 0.2% from the prior quarter.

After years of growth, Canada's population growth has cooled sharply in recent quarters after the federal government tightened immigration policy and cut numbers of temporary residents. Still, upward revisions to earlier estimates thanks in part to improved counting of temporary residents wiped out what had previously been calculated for 2025 as the first annual decline in the population for the country on record.
TALKING POINT
Americans Are About to Lose Access to Cheap Gray-Market Prescriptions From Canada
By Xavier Martinez

Diamantina Cavazos, 38-year-old Dallas-based project manager, has used an online Canadian pharmacy for two years to buy a prescription drug for around $10 a week, a fraction of what it costs in the U.S.
As of next month, a loophole that allows her to personally import the medication, Xifaxan, for her painful gut condition, is closing.
She will have to pay $1,100 a week for her prescription because she couldn't get it covered by her insurer in the U.S. "I'm extremely upset," she said.

Cavazos is one of millions of Americans who use foreign mail-order pharmacies, mostly from Canada, to acquire affordable daily medications. They are facing an impending deadline that could abruptly cut off their prescription supply.

These patients are racing to stock up on medications before late October, when a rule goes into effect requiring medications mailed from abroad to go through a customs process requiring a licensed customs broker and a financial guarantee-a bar few individual mail-order prescriptions have ever had to clear.
The government is trying to crack down on illegal contraband that it says comes into the country through low-value foreign shipments that don't pay tariffs or submit data for tracking.

"There will be just a full stop of anything coming into the States," said Tim Smith, general manager of the Canadian International Pharmacy Association, a trade group of licensed Canadian pharmacies that has built much of its business on serving American patients. "These are cash-strapped, uninsured or underinsured people; many senior citizens on fixed incomes."

More than two million people in the U.S. who take prescription drugs bought them from outside the country to save money, according to a 2020 study published in JAMA Network Open, some of the most recent research available on the topic.

The practice has operated for decades in a legal gray area: technically barred under FDA rules, importers say it is rarely enforced. Customs agents have historically waved through low-value, personal-use packages rather than individually checking each one against the agency's criteria.

The U.S. government has already made these imports more difficult. Starting in August of last year, patients ordering medication by mail have had to start paying customs fees on shipments that previously arrived free of charge.
The new rule fully closes the regulatory gap on Oct. 22.
After that, prescription drugs will need to move through a formal entry process with an accountable company or person legally on the hook if a shipment doesn't qualify.
Zonos, a St. George, Utah-based company that processes customs documentation for foreign mail services, handles much of the mail moving through Canada and other countries.

That means Zonos, not customs agents at the border, will effectively decide which packages get through-by checking each one against the FDA's actual criteria for personal drug imports, most of which have gone unenforced at scale for years. Zonos didn't respond to requests for comment.

The FDA generally won't stop a personal shipment if it treats a serious illness with no good U.S. treatment, isn't marketed to American consumers, carries no unusual safety risk and comes with a doctor's note for a 90-day supply or less. Before the rule change, that was rarely checked upfront for parcels under $800 in value because of a decades-old customs exemption for low-value mail.
A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services said the FDA would continue to evaluate personal imports on a case-by-case basis.
Smith said his members have relied on the FDA's leniency for 25 years, and that the era is ending. "Rather than exercising discretion, they're going to exercise enforcement," he said.

Ken Hunter, executive director of the New Jersey-based Campaign for Personal Prescription Importation, or CPPI, said the situation turned into a "five-alarm issue" when logistics operators such as Zonos began notifying shippers of the October cutoff.

In less than two weeks, his group's membership surged by 20,000 people. The organization has fielded more than 1,000 frantic emails and coordinated more than 28,000 letters sent to members of Congress.

Hunter said many U.S. patients rely on cheaper imports for drugs they will take for life. Eliquis, a blood thinner, is one of the most commonly ordered. A 90-day supply from Canada costs less than $600-almost half the U.S. retail price on domestic discount platforms.

Many patients have told Hunter they will cut their doses, skip pills or go without their medications entirely in anticipation of the rule change. "It is just such an avalanche of fear and concern out there," he said.

Northwest Pharmacy, a British Columbia-based international drugstore, wrote in a blog post that orders placed after Oct. 9 wouldn't be guaranteed for delivery and that the company had stopped replenishing its inventory. A different online pharmacy, which urged people to stock up on as much medication as possible, said the change would put it out of business.

The rule applies to any FDA-regulated mail shipment from any country, including smaller medication pipelines from India, the United Kingdom, Australia and Turkey. It doesn't change regulations around Americans who buy medication in person while traveling.
